1761-the-role-of-the-indians-in-the-riva.line: Governor Glen of South Carolina wrote that the colony's safety depended on staying friendly with the Indian nations against French influence.
flags: names not in source or matrix: Chickasaw, Choctaw
1761-the-role-of-the-indians-in-the-riva.about: Governor Glen of South Carolina wrote this account in 1761 of the Native nations near his colony. He listed the Catawba, Cherokee, Creek, Chickasaw and Choctaw, with rough counts of their fighting men. He said the colony's safety depended on staying friendly with them, and that this meant continuing to trade and give presents.

1823-11-07-diary-entry.line: John Quincy Adams wrote that Monroe's cabinet weighed British proposals about Spain and South America, and he opposed a joint pledge.
1823-11-07-diary-entry.about: John Quincy Adams, then Secretary of State, wrote this entry on 7 November 1823 after a Cabinet meeting at the President's. The Cabinet discussed a British proposal about European powers and South America. Adams argued the United States should not tie itself to Britain, and should state its own position to Russia and France instead. The meeting ended without a decision.

1917-04-02-speech-for-declaration-of-war.line: President Wilson asked a joint session of Congress to declare war on Germany after its submarines sank ships, and Congress then voted for war.
1917-04-02-speech-for-declaration-of-war.about: President Woodrow Wilson gave this address to a joint session of Congress on 2 April 1917 and asked for a declaration of war against Germany. He pointed to Germany's submarine warfare against ships. He said the country would fight for democracy and for the rights of small nations. Congress then voted, and the United States entered World War I.

1941-01-06-four-freedoms-speech.line: President Roosevelt told Congress the United States should aid Britain and build up arms, and named four freedoms all people should have.

1949-03-18-speech-for-the-north-atlantic.line: The United States and other nations signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington, agreeing an armed attack on one counts as an attack on all.

1969-01-20-first-inagural-address.line: President Nixon said at his inauguration that the nation was moving from an era of confrontation to one of negotiation.
1969-01-20-first-inagural-address.about: Richard Nixon gave this speech when he took office as President on 20 January 1969. He spoke of a country at war that wanted peace and was divided and wanted unity. He said the world was moving from confrontation to negotiation, and that America's lines of communication would be open. He also asked Americans to lower their voices.

1914-08-19-appeal-for-neutrality.about: President Woodrow Wilson addressed the American people on August 19, 1914, soon after war broke out in Europe. He urged them to stay neutral in thought as well as in action. He said the war's effect on the country would depend on what citizens said and did, and warned against taking sides out of partisanship.

1983-03-08-remarks-to-the-national-assoc.about: President Ronald Reagan spoke to the National Association of Evangelicals in Orlando, Florida, on March 8, 1983. He called the Soviet leaders the focus of evil in the modern world. He also opposed the nuclear freeze proposals, calling a freeze a dangerous fraud, and urged Americans to keep the country strong while seeking cuts in nuclear arms.

2020-02-29-agreement-for-bringing-peace-.about: The United States and the Taliban signed the Agreement for Bringing Peace to Afghanistan in Doha, Qatar, on February 29, 2020. The text names the Taliban as the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, a group the United States does not recognize as a state. The State Department published it in its series of treaties and other international acts.

1945-08-06-statement-on-the-bombing-of-h.line: President Truman announced that an American plane had dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, a Japanese Army base.
1945-08-06-statement-on-the-bombing-of-h.about: President Harry Truman issued this statement on 6 August 1945, announcing that an American airplane had dropped one atomic bomb on Hiroshima, which he called an important Japanese Army base. He said the bomb had more power than 20,000 tons of TNT. He described the secret effort to build it, and warned that Japan could expect more destruction if it did not accept American terms.

1963-08-05-limited-nuclear-test-ban-trea.line: The United States, Soviet Union and Britain signed a treaty banning nuclear tests in the air, in space and underwater.
1963-08-05-limited-nuclear-test-ban-trea.about: The United States, the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom signed this treaty on 5 August 1963. It banned nuclear weapon tests in the atmosphere, in outer space and under water. Tests underground were not covered. Other countries were later able to join it.

1981-11-18-address-on-arms-control-negot.line: Reagan offered to cancel new U.S. missiles in Europe if the Soviets dismantled their SS-20, SS-4 and SS-5 missiles.
1981-11-18-address-on-arms-control-negot.about: President Ronald Reagan spoke to the National Press Club on November 18, 1981, ahead of arms talks with the Soviet Union set to open in Geneva on November 30. He offered to cancel the U.S. deployment of Pershing II and cruise missiles if the Soviets dismantled their SS-20, SS-4 and SS-5 missiles.

2010-04-08-new-start-treaty.line: The United States and Russia signed a treaty in Prague limiting each side's long-range nuclear weapons.
2010-04-08-new-start-treaty.about: The New START Treaty is an agreement between the United States and the Russian Federation, dated 8 April 2010. It concerns the nuclear arms each country holds. It is published in the U.S. Treaties series.

2018-02-02-nuclear-posture-review.line: The Defense Department issued a Nuclear Posture Review, ordered by the President in January 2017, on keeping a safe and effective nuclear deterrent.
2018-02-02-nuclear-posture-review.about: The Nuclear Posture Review is a Department of Defense report released in early 2018. The President ordered it on January 27, 2017. It says the nuclear forces need modernizing to keep a credible deterrent, and it calls the security situation more complex than any since the end of the Cold War.

1962-10-22-report-on-soviet-missiles-in-.about: President Kennedy gave this television address on October 22, 1962. He said surveillance had shown offensive missile sites being prepared in Cuba, built with Soviet help. He announced a strict quarantine on offensive military equipment shipped to Cuba, and said ships carrying such cargo would be turned back.

1972-06-01-report-on-the-moscow-summit.about: President Nixon spoke to a joint session of Congress on June 1, 1972, after a 13-day trip to Austria, the Soviet Union, Iran and Poland. He said the Moscow summit took a first step toward limiting nuclear arms between the two powers. He said the ABM Treaty would go to the Senate and the interim agreement on offensive weapons to both Houses.

1970-01-01-national-environmental-policy.line: Richard Nixon signed the National Environmental Policy Act on January 1, 1970, and called it his first official act of the new decade.
1970-01-01-national-environmental-policy.about: President Richard Nixon issued this statement on January 1, 1970, when he approved the National Environmental Policy Act. He called the 1970s the years America must reclaim the purity of its air, water and living environment. He praised the bill's sponsors and said a three-member council of environmental advisers would be appointed.

1970-12-31-clean-air-act-amendments-of-1.line: Congress passed the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1970, which the president signed on December 31 and which called for national air quality standards.
1970-12-31-clean-air-act-amendments-of-1.about: The Clean Air Act Amendments of 1970 are a law passed by the U.S. Congress and dated 31 December 1970. It is listed as Public Law 91-604. The law concerns air quality and pollution.

1988-06-23-testimony-on-the-greenhouse-e.about: On June 23, 1988, NASA scientist James Hansen testified before the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. His subject was the greenhouse effect and global climate change. He told the senators that the planet was warming and tied that warming to heat-trapping gases in the air.

2015-12-12-paris-agreement.about: The Paris Agreement was adopted on December 12, 2015, under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. It is an agreement among countries to deal with climate change. Each country sets its own national plans for cutting emissions.

2022-08-16-inflation-reduction-act.about: The Inflation Reduction Act became Public Law 117-169 on August 16, 2022, when President Joe Biden signed it after Congress passed it. The law included tax credits and spending aimed at clean energy. It also contained health care and tax provisions.
flags: names not in source or matrix: Biden

1774-02-11-letter-to-rev-samson-occom.line: Phillis Wheatley wrote to the Rev. Samson Occom that she agreed with his reasons on the natural rights of Black people.
1774-02-11-letter-to-rev-samson-occom.about: Phillis Wheatley wrote this letter on February 11, 1774, to Samson Occom, a Mohegan minister. Wheatley had been brought to Boston as an enslaved girl. She agreed with his reasons on the natural rights of Black people. She wrote that love of freedom is in every human breast. Newspapers printed it that spring.

1832-09-21-franklin-hall-address.line: Maria W. Stewart spoke at Franklin Hall in Boston, calling for civil rights for northern Black people and questioning emigration to Africa.
1832-09-21-franklin-hall-address.about: Maria W. Stewart gave this lecture on September 21, 1832, at Franklin Hall in Boston. She was a free Black woman, and her audience included men, which was unusual for a woman speaker then. She called for civil rights for Northern Black people and questioned the push to send them to Africa. William Lloyd Garrison printed it in The Liberator.

1854-01-30-speech-in-the-senate.line: Senator Stephen Douglas defended his Kansas-Nebraska bill on the Senate floor, arguing that each territory's people should decide the question of slavery themselves.
1854-01-30-speech-in-the-senate.about: Senator Stephen A. Douglas of Illinois gave this speech on January 30, 1854, in defense of his Kansas-Nebraska bill. The bill let people in the new territories decide for themselves whether to allow slavery. It also repealed the Missouri Compromise line. Critics had protested, and Douglas answered them on the Senate floor.

1864-08-05-the-wade-davis-manifesto.line: Ben Wade and H. Winter Davis published a manifesto attacking the President's July 18 proclamation on a bill he had not signed.
1864-08-05-the-wade-davis-manifesto.about: Senator Benjamin Wade and Representative Henry Winter Davis published this open letter on 5 August 1864. They objected to President Lincoln's 18 July proclamation, which declined to sign their Reconstruction bill. They called his action an overreach of executive power and said Congress, not the President, should handle political reorganization of the rebel states.

1873-04-14-slaughterhouse-cases-scotus.line: The Supreme Court upheld a Louisiana slaughterhouse monopoly, ruling that the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments were passed to give former slaves full equality.
1873-04-14-slaughterhouse-cases-scotus.about: In 1873 the Supreme Court ruled on a Louisiana law that gave one New Orleans company a slaughterhouse monopoly. Butchers who lost their trade sued under the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments. The Court upheld the law. It read the amendments as meant mainly to secure equality for former slaves and limited the Privileges or Immunities Clause to rights tied to the federal government.

1941-06-25-executive-order-8802.line: Franklin Roosevelt signed an order banning racial discrimination in defense industry hiring and created a Committee on Fair Employment Practice to investigate complaints.
1941-06-25-executive-order-8802.about: President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed this order on 25 June 1941. It barred discrimination by race, creed, color or national origin in defense industries and government work. It required defense contracts to include a no-discrimination clause and created a Committee on Fair Employment Practice to investigate complaints. Roosevelt issued it after labor leader A. Philip Randolph agreed to call off a planned march on Washington.

1776-03-31-letter-to-john-adams-remember.about: Abigail Adams wrote a letter to her husband John Adams from Braintree, Massachusetts, on March 31, 1776. Most of it covers the war and the return to Boston. Near the end she says she hopes he has declared independence, and asks him to "Remember the Ladies" in the new laws and not give husbands unlimited power.

1777-01-13-petition-to-the-massachusetts.about: In January 1777, Prince Hall, a free Black man in Boston, presented a petition for freedom to the Massachusetts legislature on behalf of enslaved African Americans. It argued that they had a "natural & inalienable right" to freedom, given equally to all people. The legislature did not grant it in 1777.

1858-08-21-lincoln-douglas-debates.about: Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas held a series of public debates in Illinois in 1858 while competing for a seat in the U.S. Senate. The main subject was whether slavery should be allowed to spread into the western territories. The text is collected in Hofstadter's Great Issues in American History.
flags: names not in source or matrix: Illinois

1895-09-atlanta-exposition-address.about: Booker T. Washington gave this speech at the Cotton States Exposition in Atlanta in September 1895. He told Black and white Southerners to "Cast down your bucket where you are," urged Black Americans to begin in farming and trades, and said the races could be "as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand."

1986-06-30-bowers-v-hardwick.about: In Bowers v. Hardwick, decided in 1986, the Supreme Court heard a challenge to a Georgia law that made sodomy a crime. Michael Hardwick had been charged after a police officer saw him with another adult in his bedroom. A divided Court held that the Constitution did not protect the act. It was overruled in 2003.

1786-01-16-virginia-statute-for-religiou.line: Virginia's General Assembly passed a law, drafted by Thomas Jefferson, saying no one could be forced to support or attend any religious worship.
1786-01-16-virginia-statute-for-religiou.about: The Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom was written by Thomas Jefferson and dated 16 January 1786. It came from the Virginia General Assembly. It deals with religion and the freedom of belief.

1805-reply-to-the-rev-jacob-cram.line: Red Jacket, a Seneca leader, answered a missionary from the Boston Missionary Society who had asked the Six Nations to accept his religion.
1805-reply-to-the-rev-jacob-cram.about: In November 1805, at a council at Buffalo Creek, the Seneca leader Red Jacket (Sagoyewatha) answered a missionary from the Boston Missionary Society. The missionary had said there was one right way to worship. Red Jacket replied that his people had their own religion from their fathers, asked why white people disagreed among themselves about theirs, and said the Seneca wished only to keep their own.

1962-06-25-engel-v-vitale.line: The Supreme Court ruled that public schools could not hold a prayer authorized by New York's Board of Regents, even though taking part was voluntary.
1962-06-25-engel-v-vitale.about: In Engel v. Vitale, decided 25 June 1962, the Supreme Court ruled on a short prayer that the New York Board of Regents had approved for public schools each morning. Students did not have to take part, and the prayer named no particular faith. In an opinion by Justice Hugo Black, the Court held that the state could not hold prayers in public schools. Justice Stewart dissented.

1963-06-17-abington-school-district-v-sc.about: In 1963 the Supreme Court ruled on Bible reading in public schools. A Pennsylvania law required it each school day, and a Maryland city rule called for Bible reading and the Lord's Prayer. The Court held that public schools cannot sponsor these exercises under the First Amendment's Establishment Clause. Justice Stewart dissented.

1972-05-15-wisconsin-v-yoder.about: Wisconsin v. Yoder is a 1972 Supreme Court case (406 U.S. 205). Amish parents were prosecuted under a Wisconsin law requiring children to attend school until age 16, after they kept their children out of school following the eighth grade for religious reasons. Chief Justice Warren Burger wrote for the Court that the parents' free exercise of religion outweighed the state's interest in schooling beyond the eighth grade.

1993-11-16-religious-freedom-restoration.about: Congress passed the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, and it became law on November 16, 1993 (Pub. L. 103-141). It says government may not substantially burden a person's exercise of religion, even under a rule that applies to everyone, unless it shows a compelling interest and uses the least restrictive means. The Act names Sherbert v. Verner and Wisconsin v. Yoder as the tests it aims to restore.

1916-09-01-keating-owen-child-labor-act.line: Congress barred the interstate shipment of goods made in mines using children under sixteen, or in factories using children under fourteen.
1916-09-01-keating-owen-child-labor-act.about: Congress passed this law on 1 September 1916 to stop interstate shipment of goods made by child labor. It barred goods from mines and quarries that used children under sixteen, and from factories that used children under fourteen. Fourteen- and fifteen-year-olds could work no more than eight hours a day or six days a week. The Secretary of Labor could inspect workplaces.

1918-06-03-hammer-v-dagenhart-scotus.line: The Supreme Court struck down the Keating-Owen Child Labor Act, ruling that production was not commerce and that regulating it belonged to the states.
1918-06-03-hammer-v-dagenhart-scotus.about: The Supreme Court decided this case on 3 June 1918. Roland Dagenhart sued so his fourteen-year-old son Reuben could keep working in a textile mill, challenging the Keating-Owen Child Labor Act. Justice Day, for the majority, held the law invalid. He wrote that production is not commerce, and that the Tenth Amendment left regulating production to the states.

1935-08-14-social-security-act.line: Congress passed the Social Security Act, signed by President Franklin Roosevelt, creating national old-age insurance and federal aid to states for unemployment and dependent children.
flags: names not in source or matrix: Franklin, Large, Roosevelt, Statutes
1935-08-14-social-security-act.about: Congress passed the Social Security Act on 14 August 1935, and President Franklin Roosevelt signed it. It set up a national program of retirement payments for older workers and a system of unemployment insurance run with the states. It also gave federal money to states to help needy children and other groups. It is recorded in the Statutes at Large at 49 Stat. 620.

1971-12-09-veto-of-the-economic-opportun.about: On December 9, 1971, President Richard Nixon vetoed S. 2007, the Economic Opportunity Amendments of 1971, which would have extended the anti-poverty law, created a National Legal Services Corporation, and set up a child development program. In his veto message he objected to the child development program on grounds including cost and a belief that it would move away from strengthening parental authority and involvement with children.

1993-02-05-family-and-medical-leave-act.about: Congress passed the Family and Medical Leave Act in 1993 (Pub. L. 103-3), and President Bill Clinton signed it. It allows eligible employees to take unpaid, job-protected leave for events such as the birth or adoption of a child or a serious health condition in the family.
flags: names not in source or matrix: Bill, Clinton

2000-06-05-troxel-v-granville.about: Troxel v. Granville is a 2000 Supreme Court case (530 U.S. 57). A Washington law let any person ask a court for visitation with a child, and the paternal grandparents of two girls used it to seek more time than their mother, Tommie Granville, allowed. In a 6-3 decision, the Court held that the law violated parents' Fourteenth Amendment right to decide their children's care, custody, and control.

1790-report-on-the-public-credit.line: Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton urged Congress to pay the national war debt in full and to have the federal government take over the states' debts.
flags: names not in source or matrix: Revolutionary
1790-report-on-the-public-credit.about: Alexander Hamilton, the first Secretary of the Treasury, wrote this report for Congress in January 1790. It dealt with the debts the country had run up during the Revolutionary War. Hamilton argued that the federal government should pay those debts in full. He also proposed that the federal government take over the war debts of the states.

1877-03-01-munn-v-illinois.line: The Supreme Court ruled that Illinois could cap rates charged by grain warehouses and elevators, since states may regulate property serving the public good.
flags: names not in source or matrix: Justice
1877-03-01-munn-v-illinois.about: The Supreme Court decided this case in 1877. Illinois had set maximum rates that grain warehouses and elevators could charge. The owners said the rates denied them equal protection and due process under the 14th Amendment. The Court disagreed. Chief Justice Waite wrote that states may regulate private property "when such regulation becomes necessary for the public good."

1910-the-old-order-changeth.line: William Allen White published The Old Order Changeth, a book about American democracy, issued by Macmillan in New York.
1910-the-old-order-changeth.about: William Allen White, a writer born in 1868 and dead by 1944, published this book in 1910. Its full title is The Old Order Changeth: A View of American Democracy. Macmillan of New York was the publisher. The Internet Archive copy, scanned from a University of California library, runs 288 pages and is filed under democracy and American politics and social conditions.

1932-09-23-commonwealth-club-speech.line: Franklin Roosevelt gave a campaign speech on progressive government to the Commonwealth Club in San Francisco.
1932-09-23-commonwealth-club-speech.about: The Commonwealth Club Speech was given by Franklin Roosevelt on 23 September 1932. It is a political speech about government. It is reprinted in Hofstadter's Great Issues in American History.

1971-08-23-confidential-memorandum-attac.line: Lewis Powell Jr. wrote a confidential memorandum to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Education Committee titled Attack on American Free Enterprise System.
1971-08-23-confidential-memorandum-attac.about: Lewis F. Powell Jr. wrote this confidential memorandum on 23 August 1971 for the Education Committee of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Its title is Attack on American Free Enterprise System. Washington and Lee University School of Law keeps it in the Powell Archives, in typescript and printed copies. The archive lists its subjects as commerce and free enterprise.

1837-charles-river-bridge-v-warren-bridg.about: Charles River Bridge v. Warren Bridge was a Supreme Court case decided in 1837. Massachusetts had let one company build a toll bridge in 1785, then let another build a free bridge nearby in 1828. By 5 to 2, the Court held the first charter did not bar a second bridge, and put the community's interest in new travel and trade first.

1980-10-28-debate-between-carter-and-rea.about: President Jimmy Carter and challenger Ronald Reagan met in a televised presidential debate in Cleveland on October 28, 1980. It took place about a week before the election. The two men set out their different views of what government should do.
flags: names not in source or matrix: Cleveland, Jimmy, Ronald

1882-05-06-chinese-exclusion-act.line: Congress passed an act suspending the coming of Chinese laborers to the United States for ten years and fining ship masters who brought them.
1882-05-06-chinese-exclusion-act.about: The Chinese Exclusion Act is a law passed by the U.S. Congress and dated 6 May 1882. It is found at 22 Stat. 58. The law limited immigration from China.

1942-08-04-mexican-farm-labor-agreement.line: The United States and Mexico agreed to recruit Mexican farm workers in Mexico for temporary work in the United States.
1942-08-04-mexican-farm-labor-agreement.about: The United States and Mexico made this agreement on 4 August 1942 to let Mexican farm workers work in the United States for a set time. The linked text is the revision of 26 April 1943, made by an exchange of notes. It says Mexican workers could not be used in military service or face discrimination, and that employers would cover their transport and food.

1982-06-15-plyler-v-doe.line: The Supreme Court struck down a Texas law that let the state withhold school funds for educating children who were in the country illegally.
1982-06-15-plyler-v-doe.about: The Supreme Court decided this case on 15 June 1982. A 1975 Texas law let the state withhold school funds for educating children who were in the country illegally. The Court ruled that the law broke the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. It said these children are people under that clause, and Texas had not shown a compelling interest, so it struck the law down.

1924-05-26-immigration-act-of-1924.about: The Immigration Act of 1924 was passed by Congress and signed in May of that year. It limited immigration by national origin, with quotas that favored people from northern and western Europe. It also shut out most immigrants from Asia.

1986-11-06-immigration-reform-and-contro.about: On November 6, 1986, President Ronald Reagan signed the Immigration Reform and Control Act and issued a statement about it. He called it the most comprehensive reform of immigration laws since 1952. He said the act had three parts: penalties for employers, more enforcement, and legalization for some people already in the country.

2012-06-25-arizona-v-united-states.about: In Arizona v. United States, decided June 25, 2012, the Supreme Court ruled on four parts of Arizona's 2010 immigration law, S.B. 1070. By a 5-3 vote, with Justice Kennedy writing, it held that federal law overrode three of them. It upheld the fourth, which lets state officers check immigration status during lawful arrests.

1950-04-14-nsc-68-objectives-and-program.line: The National Security Council delivered a report to President Truman setting out U.S. objectives and programs for national security.
1950-04-14-nsc-68-objectives-and-program.about: NSC-68 is a report by the National Security Council dated 14 April 1950. Its title says it sets out objectives and programs for national security. It is published through The White House.

1951-04-19-address-to-congress.line: General Douglas MacArthur spoke to a joint meeting of the House and Senate in the House chamber on April 19.
1951-04-19-address-to-congress.about: General of the Army Douglas MacArthur gave this speech to a joint meeting of the House and Senate on 19 April 1951, in the House chamber. It was printed as Senate Document 82-36. The Library of Congress catalog lists its subjects as the Korean War, communism, and military readiness.

1951-06-01-testimony-on-the-military-sit.line: Secretary of State Dean Acheson testified to Senate committees in hearings on the Far East military situation and General MacArthur's recall.
1951-06-01-testimony-on-the-military-sit.about: Secretary of State Dean Acheson gave this testimony on 1 June 1951. It is part of Senate hearings by the Armed Services Committee, joined by the Foreign Relations Committee. The hearings looked at the Korean War, the reasons General Douglas MacArthur was recalled from his Far East command, and what the recall meant for the war.

1953-07-27-korean-armistice-agreement.about: The Korean Armistice Agreement was signed on July 27, 1953, by the United Nations Command, North Korea and China. It stopped the fighting in the Korean War and set a military line with a demilitarized zone along it. It was a ceasefire, not a peace treaty.

1994-10-21-agreed-framework-with-north-k.about: The Agreed Framework was an October 1994 deal between the United States and North Korea. North Korea agreed to freeze its plutonium-producing nuclear program. The United States agreed to arrange light-water reactors for North Korea and to supply fuel oil in the meantime.

2018-06-12-joint-statement-of-the-singap.about: On June 12, 2018, President Donald Trump of the United States and Chairman Kim Jong Un of North Korea met in Singapore and issued a joint statement. In it, the two countries committed to build new relations and a lasting peace regime on the Korean Peninsula. North Korea committed to work toward complete denuclearization, and both sides committed to recover POW/MIA remains.

1914-the-themes-of-muckraking.line: Walter Lippmann wrote an essay on the themes of muckraking, the reform journalism that exposed business and political corruption in the early 1900s.
1914-the-themes-of-muckraking.about: "The Themes of Muckraking" is a piece written by Walter Lippmann in 1914. It discusses muckraking, the style of journalism that exposed wrongdoing. It is reprinted in Hofstadter's Great Issues in American History.

1919-11-10-abrams-v-u-s-scotus.line: The Supreme Court upheld the Espionage Act convictions of defendants who threw antiwar leaflets from a New York window, over a dissent by Justice Holmes.
1919-11-10-abrams-v-u-s-scotus.about: The Supreme Court decided Abrams v. United States on 10 November 1919. Defendants were convicted under the Espionage Act for leaflets thrown from a New York window that opposed sending troops to Russia and urged a strike in ammunition plants. The Court upheld the convictions. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes dissented, saying the leaflets posed no clear and present danger.

1931-06-01-near-v-minnesota.line: The Supreme Court struck down Minnesota's law that let officials stop a newspaper from publishing, calling it a prior restraint under the First Amendment.
1931-06-01-near-v-minnesota.about: Near v. Minnesota was decided by the U.S. Supreme Court on 1 June 1931. Minnesota had used a public nuisance law to shut down The Saturday Press, a Minneapolis paper that accused local officials of ties to gangsters. Chief Justice Charles Hughes wrote that the law was a prior restraint and violated the First Amendment. Four justices dissented.

1963-03-09-new-york-times-co-v-sullivan.about: The case began with a New York Times ad that raised money to defend Martin Luther King Jr. L.B. Sullivan, an Alabama city commissioner, sued the Times for libel over it, and a jury awarded him $500,000. The Supreme Court ruled unanimously for the Times, holding that a public figure must show the false statement was made knowingly or with reckless disregard for its truth.

1969-06-09-red-lion-broadcasting-co-v-fc.about: Red Lion Broadcasting Co. v. FCC was a Supreme Court case about the FCC's fairness doctrine, which required radio and television broadcasters to present balanced discussion of public issues. Red Lion challenged how it was applied to one broadcast. The Court ruled unanimously that the rules were consistent with the First Amendment, with Justice White pointing to the scarcity of the broadcast spectrum.

1996-02-08-telecommunications-act-of-199.about: The Telecommunications Act of 1996 is a federal law passed by the U.S. Congress and signed by President Clinton on February 8, 1996. It rewrote federal rules for telephone, cable, and broadcast companies, including limits on how many stations one company could own.
flags: names not in source or matrix: Clinton

1919-10-28-national-prohibition-act.line: Congress passed the National Prohibition Act over President Wilson's veto, setting out how the ban on alcoholic drinks would be enforced.
flags: names not in source or matrix: Volstead
1919-10-28-national-prohibition-act.about: The National Prohibition Act was passed by Congress and became law on 28 October 1919. Known as the Volstead Act, it set the rules for enforcing the national ban on making and selling intoxicating liquor. It also set penalties for breaking that ban.

1966-06-13-miranda-v-arizona.line: The Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that police must warn suspects in custody of their right to remain silent and to have a lawyer before questioning.
1966-06-13-miranda-v-arizona.about: Miranda v. Arizona was decided by the Supreme Court on 13 June 1966, by a 5-4 vote. Ernesto Miranda had confessed to police after two hours of questioning without being told of his right to a lawyer. Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote that suspects in custody must be warned that they can stay silent and have an attorney. Four justices dissented.

1968-03-02-report-on-the-commission-on-c.line: The National Advisory Commission on Civil Disorders issued a report on the 1967 civil disorders, with recommendations on police-community relations and social conditions.
1968-03-02-report-on-the-commission-on-c.about: The Kerner Commission, formally the National Advisory Commission on Civil Disorders, studied the causes of the civil disorders of 1967. Its report includes a history of Black Americans in American society and a city-by-city account of that summer's disorders. It also makes recommendations on police-community relations and on justice under emergency conditions.

1961-06-19-mapp-v-ohio.about: Mapp v. Ohio is a 1961 U.S. Supreme Court case. Dollree Mapp was convicted of having obscene materials found when police searched her home for a fugitive without a valid basis. The Court ruled that evidence taken in a search that breaks the Fourth Amendment cannot be used in a state court. Justice Tom C. Clark wrote the majority opinion, and Justice Harlan dissented.

1963-03-18-gideon-v-wainwright.about: Gideon v. Wainwright is a 1963 U.S. Supreme Court case. Clarence Earl Gideon was charged with a felony in Florida, asked for a lawyer he could not afford, and was refused because Florida appointed lawyers only in capital cases. He was convicted and sentenced to five years. In a unanimous opinion by Justice Hugo Black, the Court held that state courts must appoint lawyers for defendants who cannot pay.

1994-09-13-violent-crime-control-and-law.about: The Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act is a federal law, Pub. L. 103-322, passed by Congress and signed by President Bill Clinton on September 13, 1994. It covered many parts of crime policy. It paid for more police officers, banned certain semi-automatic firearms, and added more federal crimes that could bring the death penalty.

1764-11-14-resolution-on-colonial-author.line: Virginia's House of Burgesses resolved to petition the King, the Lords and the Commons, saying colonists should be taxed only by representatives they chose.
flags: names not in source or matrix: Virginians
1764-11-14-resolution-on-colonial-author.about: On 14 November 1764 the Virginia House of Burgesses resolved to send an address to the King and memorials to Parliament. It said laws on the colony's internal government and taxes should not be imposed by any power other than the colonists' own representatives. It also said Virginians were already heavily taxed after the late war.

1774-10-14-declaration-and-resolves.line: The First Continental Congress declared that colonists were entitled to life, liberty and property, and to make their own tax laws in colonial legislatures.
1774-10-14-declaration-and-resolves.about: The First Continental Congress adopted this declaration in Philadelphia on 14 October 1774. Delegates from twelve colonies listed what Parliament had done, including taxes, the Boston port act and standing armies in peacetime. They resolved that colonists were entitled to life, liberty and property, and to make their own laws on taxation. They also chose peaceful measures, starting with a non-importation agreement.

1776-07-04-declaration-of-independence.line: Congress issued the unanimous Declaration of the thirteen United States, separating the colonies from Great Britain and listing grievances against the King.
1776-07-04-declaration-of-independence.about: The Declaration of Independence was adopted by Congress on 4 July 1776, in the name of the thirteen united States of America. It says governments get their just powers from the consent of the governed. It then lists a series of injuries it blames on the King of Great Britain, to explain why the colonies were separating.

1788-debate-in-the-virginia-ratifying-co.line: Delegates at Virginia's convention in 1788 debated whether to ratify the new federal Constitution, and the convention voted to approve it that June.
1788-debate-in-the-virginia-ratifying-co.about: The Debate in the Virginia Ratifying Convention took place on 4 and 5 June 1788. It was a debate among delegates at Virginia's convention on the Constitution. It is reprinted in Hofstadter's Great Issues in American History.

1964-06-15-reynolds-v-sims-scotus-dissen.line: Justice Harlan dissented when the Court struck down Alabama's legislative districts, arguing the Fourteenth Amendment was not meant to protect voting rights.
1964-06-15-reynolds-v-sims-scotus-dissen.about: Reynolds v. Sims was a 1964 Supreme Court case about Alabama's legislative districts. In an 8-to-1 decision, the Court held that both houses of a state legislature must be apportioned by population. Justice Harlan dissented. He argued the Fourteenth Amendment was not meant to protect voting rights and that the Court was intruding on the states.

1765-the-objections-to-the-taxations-con.about: This is a 1765 pamphlet by Soame Jenyns, first published without his name. Its full title is The Objections to the Taxation of Our American Colonies, by the Legislature of Great Britain, Briefly Consider'd. It takes up the objections raised against Parliament taxing the American colonies.

1775-07-06-declaration-of-the-causes-and.about: The Second Continental Congress issued this declaration on July 6, 1775, to explain why the colonies had taken up arms against Britain. It says the colonists took up arms to defend their freedom and property. They said they would lay the arms down when hostilities ceased and the danger of their return was removed. It was written mainly by Thomas Jefferson and John Dickinson.

1828-12-19-south-carolina-protest-agains.line: South Carolina's House of Representatives received an Exposition and Protest against the Tariff of 1828, written by John C. Calhoun, which threatened secession if the tariff was not repealed.
1828-12-19-south-carolina-protest-agains.about: The South Carolina Exposition and Protest was written in 1828 by John C. Calhoun, then Vice President, who kept his authorship hidden. It protested the Tariff of 1828 and said a state could reject federal law. It was presented to the South Carolina House on December 19, 1828. The legislature did not formally adopt it, but a pamphlet was printed.

1892-07-04-populist-party-platform.line: The People's Party of America held its first national convention on the Fourth of July and issued a platform describing a nation near ruin, with labor impoverished and land held by capitalists.
1892-07-04-populist-party-platform.about: The People's Party adopted this platform at its first national convention on July 4, 1892. It describes a country in ruin, with money and land in the hands of a few. It demands a graduated income tax, free coinage of silver and gold at a ratio of 16 to 1, and postal savings banks run by the government.

1971-08-15-address-on-the-economy.line: President Richard Nixon told the nation he was ordering a 90-day freeze on prices and wages and suspending the dollar's convertibility into gold.
1971-08-15-address-on-the-economy.about: On August 15, 1971, President Richard Nixon went on television to announce a new economic policy. He ordered a freeze on all prices and wages for 90 days. He added a 10 percent tax on imported goods. He also suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold, which he called a defense against international speculators.

1905-04-17-lochner-v-new-york-scotus.about: Lochner v. New York was a Supreme Court case decided in 1905. New York's Bakeshop Act barred bakers from working more than 60 hours a week or 10 hours a day, and a bakery owner named Lochner was fined under it. The Court struck the law down, ruling that it interfered with the freedom of employer and employee to make contracts.

2019-08-18-statement-on-the-purpose-of-a.about: The Statement on the Purpose of a Corporation was released by the Business Roundtable in August 2019 and signed by 181 CEOs. It says they commit to lead their companies for the benefit of all stakeholders: customers, employees, suppliers, communities and shareholders. It replaced earlier statements that had endorsed shareholder primacy.

1795-examination-of-the-treaty-between-t.about: Robert R. Livingston wrote an examination of the treaty between the United States and Great Britain in 1795. It gives his reading of that treaty. Hofstadter included it in Great Issues in American History.

1947-the-sources-of-soviet-conduct.about: George F. Kennan wrote The Sources of Soviet Conduct in 1947. It appeared in July of that year. It discusses where Soviet behavior came from and what that meant for the United States. Hofstadter included it in Great Issues in American History.

2026-02-05-expiration-of-the-new-start-t.about: This entry covers the end of the New START Treaty, an arms control agreement between the United States and Russia. The entry is dated 5 February 2026. The source is the Department of State.
flags: names not in source or matrix: Department

1970-declaration-of-environmental-rights.line: A Declaration of Environmental Rights was issued in 1970 as a public statement of rights concerning the environment.
flags: names not in source or matrix: Yale
1970-declaration-of-environmental-rights.about: The Declaration of Environmental Rights is a statement from 1970 about people's rights in relation to the natural environment. It is printed in Hofstadter's collection Great Issues in American History. The linked copy is hosted by Yale's energy history site.

1825-12-06-first-annual-message-to-congr.line: President John Quincy Adams sent his first annual message to Congress on 6 December 1825.
1825-12-06-first-annual-message-to-congr.about: The First Annual Message to Congress was delivered by John Quincy Adams on 6 December 1825. It is a message from the president to Congress. It is reprinted in Hofstadter's Great Issues in American History.

1790-12-16-on-the-assumption-of-state-de.about: The Virginia Resolutions On the Assumption of State Debts are dated 16 December 1790. They address the question of the national government taking on the debts of the states. Hofstadter included them in Great Issues in American History.

1913-experiments-in-government.about: Elihu Root wrote Experiments in Government in 1913. As the title says, it deals with experiments in how government is run. Hofstadter included it in Great Issues in American History.

2023-04-mandate-for-leadership-the-conse.about: The Heritage Foundation published Mandate for Leadership: The Conservative Promise in April 2023. It is a long book of policy proposals for the federal government. The Foundation posted the full text as a PDF.

1787-11-22-the-federalist-nos-10-and-15.about: James Madison and Alexander Hamilton wrote The Federalist Nos. 10 and 15 in 1787. The Federalist essays were written in support of the proposed Constitution. The entry is dated 22 November 1787.

1974-09-08-address-on-the-pardon-of-rich.about: Gerald Ford gave this address on 8 September 1974, when he was president. It concerns his pardon of Richard Nixon. Hofstadter included it in Great Issues in American History.

2024-07-01-trump-v-united-states.about: Trump v. United States is a case decided by the Supreme Court on 1 July 2024. It concerned whether a former president is immune from criminal prosecution. The case involved Donald Trump.

1955-01-29-formosa-resolution.line: Congress passed the Formosa Resolution on 29 January 1955, authorizing the President to use American armed forces to defend Formosa.
flags: names not in source or matrix: Large, Statutes
1955-01-29-formosa-resolution.about: The Formosa Resolution was a joint resolution of the U.S. Congress. It was passed on 29 January 1955. It authorized the President to use American armed forces to defend Formosa. It appears in the Statutes at Large.

1972-02-27-the-shanghai-communique.line: The United States and China issued the Shanghai Communique on 27 February 1972, a joint statement that addressed Taiwan among other subjects.
1972-02-27-the-shanghai-communique.about: The Shanghai Communique was a joint statement by the United States and China, dated 27 February 1972. It dealt with relations between the two countries, including the question of Taiwan. Hofstadter included it in Great Issues in American History.

2005-03-14-anti-secession-law.line: China's National People's Congress adopted the Anti-Secession Law on 14 March 2005, a law about Taiwan.
2005-03-14-anti-secession-law.about: The Anti-Secession Law was passed by China's National People's Congress on 14 March 2005. It is a Chinese law about Taiwan. Its text is published by the National People's Congress.

1776-03-09-of-colonies-from-the-wealth-o.line: Adam Smith published The Wealth of Nations in 1776, and the book included a chapter titled Of Colonies.
1776-03-09-of-colonies-from-the-wealth-o.about: "Of Colonies" is a section of The Wealth of Nations by Adam Smith. The book was published on 9 March 1776. The section discusses colonies and how they relate to the countries that rule them. It is reprinted in Hofstadter's Great Issues in American History.

1896-07-08-cross-of-gold-speech.line: William Jennings Bryan gave the Cross of Gold speech on 8 July 1896.
1896-07-08-cross-of-gold-speech.about: The Cross of Gold Speech was given by William Jennings Bryan on 8 July 1896. It is a political speech about money. It is reprinted in Hofstadter's Great Issues in American History.

1776-03-09-conclusion-of-the-mercantile-.about: Adam Smith wrote the Conclusion of the Mercantile System in 1776. It is a chapter of The Wealth of Nations. It closes his discussion of the mercantile system, a set of ideas about trade and national wealth. Hofstadter included it in Great Issues in American History.

1888-looking-backward.about: Looking Backward is a novel by Edward Bellamy, published in 1888. It imagines a future American society. Hofstadter included it in Great Issues in American History.

1999-11-12-gramm-leach-bliley-act.about: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act is a federal law passed by Congress. It became Public Law 106-102 and is dated 12 November 1999. It dealt with the financial industry.

1940-12-17-press-conference-on-lend-leas.line: Franklin Roosevelt told reporters the United States could take over British munitions orders and lend or lease the goods, to be repaid in kind after the war.
1940-12-17-press-conference-on-lend-leas.about: President Franklin Roosevelt held this press conference on 17 December 1940. He said the best defense of the United States was for Britain to succeed in defending itself. He proposed lending munitions instead of selling them for money, and compared it to lending a neighbor a garden hose to fight a fire. If the hose came back damaged, the neighbor would replace it.

1947-06-05-the-marshall-plan.line: Secretary of State George Marshall told Harvard graduates that the United States should help Europe recover from the war, through a plan the Europeans would draw up.
1947-06-05-the-marshall-plan.about: Secretary of State George C. Marshall gave this speech at Harvard on 5 June 1947. He described the economic crisis in Europe after World War II and said the United States should help the region recover. He said the aid was aimed at hunger, poverty and chaos, not at any country. Europeans were to draw up a recovery plan and present it to the United States.

1941-12-08-war-message-to-congress.about: President Franklin Roosevelt gave this speech to Congress on 8 December 1941, the day after Japanese forces attacked Hawaii. He described attacks across the Pacific, including Malaya, Guam, the Philippines, Wake Island and Midway. He asked Congress to declare that a state of war existed between the United States and the Japanese Empire.
flags: names not in source or matrix: Philippines

1978-09-18-address-on-the-camp-david-acc.about: President Jimmy Carter spoke to a joint session of Congress on 18 September 1978, after two weeks of talks at Camp David with Egypt's Anwar Sadat and Israel's Menahem Begin. He described two agreements. One was a framework for peace in the Middle East. The other was a framework for a peace treaty between Egypt and Israel, which returned the Sinai Peninsula to Egyptian sovereignty.

1954-05-17-brown-v-board-of-education-of.about: On 17 May 1954 the Supreme Court decided Brown v. Board of Education, which combined cases from Kansas, South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware and Washington, D.C. Black students had been refused admission to certain public schools under segregation laws. In a unanimous opinion by Chief Justice Earl Warren, the Court held that separate schools were inherently unequal and violated the Equal Protection Clause.

2018-06-04-masterpiece-cakeshop-v-colora.about: In Masterpiece Cakeshop, decided 4 June 2018, a Colorado baker named Jack Phillips had declined to make a wedding cake for a same-sex couple because of his religious beliefs. Colorado's civil rights bodies ruled against him. The Supreme Court reversed 7 to 2. It held that commission members showed hostility toward his beliefs, which broke the Free Exercise Clause.

1979-07-15-crisis-of-confidence-address.about: President Jimmy Carter gave this televised speech on 15 July 1979, after ten days of meeting people at Camp David. He said he had planned to talk about energy but chose to talk about what he called a crisis of confidence. He said Americans were losing faith in the future and that a majority believed the next five years would be worse than the past five.

1997-06-26-reno-v-american-civil-liberti.about: Reno v. ACLU was decided by the Supreme Court on 26 June 1997. It tested the 1996 Communications Decency Act, which made it a crime to send "obscene or indecent" messages online where minors could see them. The Court held that the Act violated the First Amendment as a content-based blanket restriction on speech. Justice O'Connor partly dissented.

2022-06-23-new-york-state-rifle-pistol-a.about: New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen was decided by the Supreme Court on 23 June 2022. New York required a person to show a special need for self-protection to get an unrestricted license to carry a concealed gun outside the home. The Court held that this rule violated the right to keep and bear arms in public for self-defense. Three justices dissented.

1979-04-10-taiwan-relations-act.about: The Taiwan Relations Act is a law passed by the U.S. Congress and signed on April 10, 1979. It lets the United States keep commercial and cultural ties with the people on Taiwan after formal relations ended. It says the U.S. expects Taiwan's future to be settled peacefully, and that it will provide Taiwan with defensive arms.

1981-08-03-remarks-on-the-air-traffic-co.about: On August 3, 1981, President Ronald Reagan spoke to reporters after the air traffic controllers' union called a strike. He said federal workers had sworn an oath not to strike and that Congress had forbidden such strikes. He told controllers who did not report for work within 48 hours that they had forfeited their jobs and would be terminated.

1983-04-a-nation-at-risk.about: A Nation at Risk is a report issued in April 1983 by the National Commission on Excellence in Education. It was published by the U.S. Department of Education. It examines the state of American schools.
